n622257d2e3b8: Active learning engages students in some activity that induces them to reflect upon ideas and how they are using these ideas. It also involves the process of keeping students mentally, and often physically, active in their learning through activities that engage them in gathering information, thinking, and solving problems. This study was conducted to determine if creating physical exhibits fosters higher-order cognitive skills like problem solving and critical thinking (application and analysis, respectively). In this study, carried out in the Department of Physiology, 50 medical undergraduate students were divided into four batches of 12–13 students each. Each batch was supervised by a faculty mentor and assigned a topic for the preparation of a physical exhibit. Multiple-choice questions (MCQ) testing higher-order cognitive skills were used to assess the gain in knowledge post-intervention. The qualitative component of the study consisted of open-ended questions and a Focus Group Discussion to ascertain students’ perceptions regarding the creation of physical exhibits. The students created physical exhibits related to the sensory pathway, the light reflex & the conjunctival reflex, the micturition reflex mechanism, and the automatic bladder. Median post-test scores showed significant improvement compared to pretest scores (16 vs 12, p < 0.01). Students reported that the active learning strategy promoted deep learning, enhanced memory, and helped them apply theory to practice. Secondly, it cultivated teamwork skills. The learning experience was enjoyable and led them to score higher on the post-test exams. Students also suggested that tightening the nuts and bolts, as in prior meticulous planning, would make the experience more enjoyable.
nbb17f9e3df96: Wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss, yet how trade interacts with species’ ecological traits and extinction risk remains underexplored. Carnivores warrant special attention because they are disproportionately exploited and vulnerable to extinction compared to other taxa. We analyzed 171,637 international trade records spanning 50 years (1975–2024) for 129 carnivore species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). We analyzed trade volumes across the globe and then used logistic regression to evaluate associations between ecological traits and extinction risk, as well as family-level differences in extinction risk. Trade volumes were dominated by exports from North America and Europe and imports concentrated in East Asia, highlighting persistent transcontinental trade. Logistic regression identified longer generation length and greater dispersal distance as positively associated with higher extinction risk, whereas broader habitat breadth was associated with lower extinction risk. Among carnivore families, only Ursidae (bears) exhibited significantly greater odds of being threatened relative to the Canidae (canids) reference family. Our findings demonstrate that ecological traits are associated with extinction risk within CITES-listed carnivores, supporting the use of trait-based approaches as a complementary tool for conservation assessment and monitoring of internationally traded species.
n97454a4fd3cf: Background Hypertension affects more than 1.28 billion adults globally and remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, renal failure, and premature death. This burden is inconsistently distributed across Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), where nearly three-quarters of adults live with hypertension. This gap is largely driven by poor adherence and low retention. This systematic review aims to assess the effectiveness of nurse-led interventions on retention in care, medication adherence, and blood pressure among adult patients with hypertension in primary health care settings in LMICs. Methods The protocol was registered (PROSPERO CRD420251136515) following the PRISMA guidelines. We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane for articles published between 2000 and 2026. Eligibility criteria included: adults (≥18 years) with hypertension receiving care from primary care clinics; nurse-led interventions; usual care as comparator; primary outcome: retention rates; secondary outcomes: medication adherence, blood pressure (BP) control. Inclusion: experimental, quasi-experimental, and prospective cohort studies. Dual independent screening and data extraction were performed. Quality assessment was performed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2(RoB2) for randomized controlled trials and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools for quasi-experimental and observational studies. Due to heterogeneity in intervention duration, outcome measures, and follow-up periods, a narrative synthesis was employed. Results Eleven unique studies (n = 19,005) were identified: 63.6% RCTs, 18.2% quasi-experimental, and 18.2% observational. Seven studies were conducted in Africa and four in Asia. The mean age range was 52.0–67.4 years; 51.3%−76.0% were female. Risk-of-bias assessment revealed high or unclear risk in the missing outcomes data domain for most RCTs. Ten studies used multicomponent interventions. Retention rates varied with appointment attendance (12.6–96.5%), routine clinical retention (27.0–62.8%), and study completion of follow-up (83.8% to 97.2%). Four studies reported medication adherence with varying effects in the intervention group compared to the control or baseline. Ten studies reported systolic blood pressure (SBP) outcomes; 9 reported mean SBP after intervention; the majority reported the mean reduction of SBP was greater than 10 mmHg. Nine studies reported diastolic blood pressure (DBP) outcomes; all studies reported a reduction in DBP after the intervention, with a range of −1.8 mmHg to −20.6 mmHg. Reported SBP and DBP reductions included both within-group controlled estimates; these should not be interpreted as a pooled effect. Conclusion This systematic review included 11 studies that showed nurse-led interventions improved blood pressure control in primary health care facilities of LMICs. But retention in care showed substantial variability in nurse-led interventions in primary health care facilities of LMICs. Nurse-led interventions in LMICs are a promising strategy for improving blood pressure control. However, retention in care was substantially and variably due to heterogeneous definitions and evidence on medication adherence was limited. Future research should prioritize standardized outcome measures and robust study designs to strengthen the evidence base and inform sustainable scale-up of these models in LMICs.
nf2ae08b8300a: People who are unable to achieve a healthy lifestyle are at greater risk of type II diabetes, some cancers, heart disease, stroke, mobility problems and poor outcomes from disease. For individuals living in disadvantaged areas, life circumstances such as low income, unemployment, working anti-social hours and limited local services present barriers to the challenge of living healthy lives. Working with two disadvantaged communities in Forth Valley, Scotland, we co-designed and implemented an evidence-informed, incentive-based intervention, Enjoy Life LocallY (ELLY), to support citizens with healthy weight and wellbeing. The intervention comprised free soup twice weekly (café/delivery/pickup); a loyalty card (stamped upon engagement in community assets such as local activities, groups and clubs) exchanged for a £25 shopping card when a minimum of 9 assets over 12 weeks were attended; goal setting; information resources; and self-monitoring of weight and wellbeing. ELLY was delivered by volunteers over a 12-week period, from September 2023 to November 2023, to 75 residents. Qualitative interviews were conducted at 12-weeks with 10 participants per community, to assess study feasibility and conceptualise pathways to how ELLY led to healthy weight and wellbeing outcomes. Data were analysed using framework analysis. The ELLY intervention demonstrated strong acceptability and feasibility and was positively received by participants. In-depth interview data informed the construction of a conceptual framework identifying pathways through which the intervention supports healthy weight and wellbeing, including positive changes in behaviour, strengthened social connectedness, improved dietary habits, measurable participant-reported health improvements and the acquisition of new skills and knowledge. Collectively, findings support the hypothesis that engagement in the ELLY intervention was associated with a range of important health outcomes for participants, making a valuable contribution to the evidence base on community-based interventions and highlighting the important role of co-designed community interventions in supporting underserved, disadvantaged communities in health improvement.
ne8d3468d9b6a: Landslides are a major rainfall-triggered hazard affecting road infrastructure across the mountainous terrain of western Panama. This study develops an ensemble Frequency Ratio (FR)-Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) modelling framework to assess landslide susceptibility, identify critical management zones, and determine key drivers of slope failure along road corridors in the mainland districts of Bocas del Toro and along the Rambala-Hornito-David route. Within a 1,000 m corridor buffer, 87 mapped landslides (63 for training and 24 for validation) and 15 environmental conditioning factors were used to develop and validate the FR and MaxEnt models. An AUC-weighted linear combination of the independently calibrated FR and MaxEnt models was used to generate the ensemble susceptibility map. The ensemble delineated 9.67% and 3.99% of the corridor as high and very high susceptibility, respectively, achieving the highest predictive performance (AUC = 0.945) and outperforming the FR (0.873) and MaxEnt (0.943) models. Sensitivity analyses based on alternative training-validation partitions (57:30 and 70:17) produced consistently good performance (prediction-rate AUC > 0.88), indicating that the principal findings were not strongly influenced by the inventory allocation. Hotspot analysis identified three major clusters of elevated susceptibility and confirmed statistically significant spatial clustering at the 95% and 99% confidence levels. More than 71 km of primary roads intersect high-susceptibility zones, with Hornito, Bajo Cedro, and Valle de Agua Arriba exhibiting the greatest exposure. Slope gradient and NDVI were identified as the most influential predictors. These findings provide a practical basis for prioritising monitoring, slope stabilisation, drainage improvement, and ecosystem-based interventions to strengthen the resilience of road infrastructure in tropical mountain environments. Future work should incorporate larger landslide inventories, event-based rainfall information, and climate-change scenarios to improve the representation of landslide dynamics and support risk-informed infrastructure planning.
ne5c83d9e2822: Topical ocular drug delivery is often restricted by rapid precorneal clearance, which can decrease drug residence time and bioavailability at the ocular surface. The purpose of the study was to develop a sulfacetamide-loaded niosomal gel (SA-Nio-Gel) to enhance ocular drug delivery. Thin film hydration method was used for the preparation of SA niosomes, employing nonionic surfactants (Span 60 and Span 80) and cholesterol. The optimized niosomal formulation was then incorporated into a Carbopol 934 gel base to prepare the final SA-Nio-Gel formulation. The optimized niosomes exhibited encapsulation efficiency of 76% ± 1.5 and a mean particle size of 129.7 ± 2.52 nm. Rheological analysis of the SA-Nio-Gel demonstrated pseudoplastic behavior, characterized by a reduction in viscosity with increasing shear rate. Biocompatibility evaluation indicated that the formulation was non-toxic. In vitro release profiles showed a slow and sustained SA release from the developed formulation. Furthermore, microbiological assays confirmed the potent antibacterial activity of the SA-Nio-Gel against S. aureus. Compared to the SA solution and SA-Nio, the SA-Nio-Gel formulation significantly minimized precorneal drainage and improved drug penetration. These results indicate that the niosomal gel-based system could be a promising platform for the ocular delivery of SA, which provides sustained release and enhanced drug permeability.
nd0fbb7096ff3: Objective To evaluate gender differences in pre-surgical motivations, expectations, functional and psychosocial evaluations, and treatment process perceptions among adult patients with skeletal Class III malocclusion undergoing orthodontic preparation for orthognathic surgery. Methods In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 81 adults (37 females, 44 males) with skeletal Class III malocclusion completed a 27-item investigator-developed questionnaire during pre-surgical orthodontic preparation, covering demographics, problem awareness, functional and psychosocial evaluations, motivation and expectations, treatment process, and patient engagement. Gender differences were analyzed item by item with Mann-Whitney U, chi-square, or Fisher’s exact tests. P-values for the 37 comparisons were adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure within questionnaire domains, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were estimated. Because the a priori sample size calculation did not address between-gender comparisons, these were treated as exploratory. Results Seven differences met the unadjusted threshold (p < 0.05), of which three remained significant after within-domain FDR correction: females reported greater lack of self-confidence in social environments (q = 0.044), and males reported more adequate information from their orthodontist (q = 0.018) and higher pre-operative treatment satisfaction (q = 0.019), with moderate effect sizes (rank-biserial |r| = 0.30–0.35). The other four, all reported more often by females (eating difficulty, food avoidance, temporomandibular joint problems, and lack of confidence when photographed), were nominally significant only (unadjusted p = 0.013–0.043). No difference survived correction across all 37 comparisons. For the other items no significant differences were detected, but confidence intervals did not exclude small-to-moderate differences. Conclusions Gender differences in social self-confidence, perceived information adequacy, and pre-operative satisfaction were the strongest exploratory findings. Because the study was not powered for gender comparisons, non-significant results do not indicate that the genders are similar. These exploratory findings warrant confirmation in adequately powered multi-center, longitudinal studies.
na036805a4114: Background Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) is a severe neurological complication of sepsis, characterized by uncontrolled neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, yet no specific therapy is currently available. Harpagide, a naturally occurring iridoid glycoside, has been reported to possess anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective activities; however, its therapeutic potential in SAE remains unexplored. This study aimed to investigate whether Harpagide exerts neuroprotective effects in SAE and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Methods A mouse model of SAE was established by intraperitoneal injection of lipopolysaccharide (LPS, 18 mg/kg). Cognitive performance was assessed using behavioral assays. Brain tissue morphology and neuronal survival were evaluated through histopathological examination. Glial cell activation and the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) were measured. Network pharmacology was employed to predict potential targets, followed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations to predict binding interactions with core targets. Western blotting was performed to determine the expression levels of key proteins involved in the MMP9/NF-κB signaling pathway. Results Treatment with Harpagide significantly improved behavioral performance, ameliorated brain pathological changes, preserved hippocampal neurons, suppressed glial activation, and reduced the levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 in SAE mice. Network pharmacology analysis predicted four core targets: GAPDH, CASP3, MMP9, and ICAM1. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested stable binding between Harpagide and MMP9. Western blot analysis further showed that Harpagide treatment was associated with reduced expression of MMP9 and phosphorylated NF-κB p65 in both hippocampal and cortical tissues. Conclusions The present study demonstrates that Harpagide exerts neuroprotective effects in SAE, which are associated with mitigated neuroinflammation and reduced MMP9/NF-κB signaling, supporting its potential as a promising therapeutic candidate for this devastating condition.
necff664ab435: Introduction Nutrition-sensitive interventions aim to improve or at least safeguard the underlying causes of malnutrition, especially among the most vulnerable populations. Integrated nutrition-sensitive interventions are effective strategies for improving household food security and dietary diversity in low-income settings. In 2021, the European Union (EU) and UNICEF, in collaboration with the Government of Bangladesh and partners, implemented nutrition-sensitive interventions combining two income-generating activities (IGAs): backyard poultry rearing and tailoring with asset transfers, direct cash support, and nutrition education for vulnerable women in the host communities of Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. We evaluated the association of these interventions with household food security and dietary diversity among vulnerable women. Materials and methods We analyzed data from two rounds (2022 and 2024) of repeated cross-sectional surveys involving 1,255 vulnerable women (638 in 2022 and 617 in 2024) across four upazilas in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Covariates were initially imbalanced across groups because the interventions were not randomly assigned; therefore, we employed propensity score weighting to balance the covariates between the two groups. We used modified Poisson regression and binomial regression models to estimate the association between exposure and outcomes from the pseudo-population obtained by propensity score weighting. All the inferences in this manuscript were based on a 5% significance level. Results In 2024, vulnerable women had a 53% higher likelihood of household food security (RR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.27–1.85, p < 0.001) than in 2022. Similarly, dietary diversity of vulnerable women increased markedly, showing over two and a half-fold higher likelihood of adequate dietary diversity in 2024 (RR = 2.78, 95% CI: 2.36–3.27, p < 0.001). The E-values corresponding to the associations of food security and dietary diversity with survey year were 2.44 and 5.00, respectively, on the risk ratio scale, which shows that the findings were less sensitive to unmeasured confounders. Conclusion Household food security and dietary diversity substantially increased over time among vulnerable women in the study areas. As the study was a two-repeated cross-sectional survey, residual confounding and other time-varying contextual factors cannot be excluded, so the observed differences should not be interpreted as definitive causal effects of the intervention. Future controlled or longitudinal evaluations are needed to establish the causal effectiveness and long-term sustainability of integrated nutrition-sensitive interventions.
n8c9f22ea9cb1: Achieving Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) is vital for the long-term sustainability of human well-being and the realisation of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 15.3.1. We estimated the overall indicator of SDG 15.3.1, the proportion of land that is degraded over the total land area in the Central Region, Malawi, from 2001 to 2022, using the Trends.Earth tool in QGIS. The study applied the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) Good Practice Guidance methodology for SDG Indicator 15.3.1 assessment, integrating land cover, land productivity, and soil organic carbon (SOC) sub-indicators. The default datasets in the Trends.Earth plugin were adopted for all sub-indicators. The study has revealed that: (i) The proportion of degraded land increased from 26.8% in the baseline period (2001–2015) to 41.2% in the monitoring period (2016–2022). Stable land area decreased from 62.2% to 55.7%, while improved land area declined from 10.0% to 2.0%. Overall, during the entire study period (2001–2022), 27.1% of the land remained degraded, 62.4% was stable, and 9.4% improved. (ii) Land with degraded productivity significantly declined from 74.5% to 29.3%. In contrast, land with stable productivity slightly increased from 1.1% to 1.9%. (iii) SOC levels remained largely stable (>97%), although slight losses occurred in cropland, grassland, and wetland areas. (iv) Land cover remained predominantly stable (96.7%) throughout the study period. The overall SDG 15.3.1 indicator indicates continued degradation trends exceeding the rate of land recovery and restoration. This study has highlighted key spatial patterns and identified insights into the priority areas for targeted LDN interventions in the Central Region of Malawi. The findings provide critical evidence for guiding sustainable land management strategies and accelerating progress toward achieving land degradation neutrality in Malawi.
n9746b8632ccc: Although temperate monsoon climate regions are traditionally known for their harsh winter climates, the combined effects of rapid urbanization and global climate change have significantly intensified summer urban heat island effects in these areas, making them a neglected yet increasingly severe challenge in high-latitude urban climate adaptation planning. This study takes a typical campus in Shenyang, a temperate monsoon climate region in Northeast China, as the experimental subject. It quantitatively dissects the non-linear statistical associations and regulatory mechanisms of biotic and abiotic landscape elements and their spatial configurations on microclimate parameters and human thermal comfort (Physiologically Equivalent Temperature, PET) by combining microclimate field observations with validated ENVI-met numerical simulations. Field measurement results show that the vertical structural characteristics of vegetation dominate cooling efficiency: evergreen trees and shrubs, with their dense radiation-blocking structures, exhibit optimal regulatory potential, with mean Physiological Equivalent Temperature (ΔPET) values reaching 10.6°C and 10.4°C, respectively, significantly outperforming deciduous trees (8.1°C). In contrast, abiotic elements play an auxiliary role, with dynamic water bodies and enclosed pavilions providing PET improvement values of 3.1°C and 2.9°C, respectively, while paving materials have limited direct regulatory capacity (< 2.0°C). Simulation optimization further reveals a significant “blue-green synergy” effect: the composite configuration of high-canopy evergreen trees and large-area dynamic water bodies forms the optimal spatial solution, reducing daily average PET to 48.7°C, a decrease of 7.3°C compared to the vegetation-free baseline scenario. Addressing the unique “humid-heat” challenge that distinguishes temperate monsoon climates from arid or semi-arid regions where summer thermal stress is often attributed solely to high temperatures, this study goes beyond merely documenting cooling effects to elucidate the “structural-thermal decoupling” mechanism in temperate monsoon climates. It challenges the conventional “deciduous-first” design paradigm by quantifying the superior radiative-blocking efficiency of evergreen species during extreme heatwaves, providing a physically-grounded framework for campus microclimate resilience.
n469f4b242f9c: Many bacteria form spores to endure unfavorable conditions. While Firmicutes generate endospores through cell division, sporulation in non-Firmicutes remains less understood. The Gram-negative bacterium Myxococcus xanthus undergoes sporulation through two distinct mechanisms: rapid sporulation triggered by chemical induction and slow sporulation driven by starvation, both occurring independently of cell division. Instead, these processes depend on the complete degradation of the peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall by two lytic transglycosylases (LTGs), LtgA and LtgB. Remarkably, LtgB programs the pace of PG degradation by LtgA during rapid sporulation, ensuring a controlled process that prevents abrupt PG breakdown and the formation of non-resistant pseudospores. In addition to regulation between LTGs, PG degradation is also influenced by its synthesis; cells exhibiting increased muropeptide production often circumvent sporulation. These findings not only reveal novel mechanisms of bacterial sporulation but also shed light on the regulatory network governing PG dynamics.
na969e165a2fb: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.
nf6c003701d7c: Heartbeat and behavior are tightly coordinated during defensive states, yet the neuronal mechanisms linking threat processing to cardiac modulation—and the potential contribution of cardiac dynamics to behavioral output—remain poorly understood. Here, using simultaneous recordings of heartbeat and behavior in tethered Drosophila, we show that mechanical threat triggers locomotion together with rapid cardiac deceleration. We identify two pairs of dopaminergic neurons, termed DA-WED neurons, that mediate this cardiac response. Silencing these neurons markedly attenuates threat-induced cardiac deceleration, whereas optogenetic activation induces cardiac deceleration in the absence of threat. Two-photon calcium imaging further shows that DA-WED neurons are activated by mechanical threat, and manipulating their activity bidirectionally modulates threat-induced locomotion. Linking cardiac dynamics to behavior, direct optogenetic manipulation of cardiomyocytes that quantitatively reproduces threat-evoked cardiac deceleration is accompanied by increased locomotion. Together, these results identify a dopaminergic descending pathway that links threat processing to cardiac modulation and suggest that cardiac dynamics may contribute to shaping defensive behavior.
na0ecbf1cd45a: Blood progenitors are regulated by a variety of systemic and nutritional cues from their environment. In the Drosophila lymph gland (LG), the Posterior Signaling Center acts as a stem cell niche striking a balance between progenitors and differentiated blood cells. Autophagy is a vital cellular process that maintains homeostasis by removing unnecessary or dysfunctional cell components through autophagic degradation and recycling. Here, using genetic perturbation analysis, we show that autophagy plays a critical role in regulating LG blood cell homeostasis. General control non-derepressible 5 (Gcn5), a histone acetyltransferase, is expressed in the primary LG lobe, and modulation of Gcn5 levels perturbs LG homeostasis. Our results show that hemocyte-specific Gcn5 modulation controls autophagic flux in the hemocytes. Furthermore, we show that modulation of mTORC1 activity can perturb hematopoiesis. Our results indicate that organismal Gcn5 levels respond to dietary shifts and are modulated by mTORC1 signaling. Chemical intervention shows that mTORC1 overrides the effect exerted by Gcn5 in regulating LG hematopoiesis. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Gcn5 and mTORC1 regulate autophagy to maintain blood cell homeostasis in Drosophila.
ne93437c9d17a: The differential microtubule organization in axons and dendrites underlies neuronal polarity and developmental processes, like neurite pruning. How neurons achieve their specific microtubule organization during development is an area of active research, and it has been especially hard to explain how dendritic microtubules are oriented with their plus ends toward the soma. Transient microtubule nucleation from tips of early growing dendrites has been proposed as a mechanism that would explain how this orientation is set up. In a survey for cytoskeletal regulators involved in dendrite pruning and microtubule organization in Drosophila, we found the spectraplakin Short stop (Shot), an actin/microtubule crosslinker. Loss of Shot causes microtubule orientation defects already during early dendrite development, when Shot is transiently recruited to tips of growing dendrites via its actin-binding domain. Genetic and functional evidence suggests that Shot’s primary function in this process is to locally stabilize microtubules. We also provide evidence for an independent, developmentally transient microtubule nucleation mechanism. Our data highlight the importance of transient and localized microtubule regulation for dendritic microtubule organization.
n01709f8f6122: Food formulation requires balancing taste, nutrition, sustainability, and cost. Traditionally, new foods have emerged through empirical experimentation, expert intuition, and iterative refinement. Now, artificial intelligence (AI) offers the opportunity to accelerate this process. Yet despite rapid advances across food science, most AI applications remain isolated prediction and optimization tasks rather than parts of a broader scientific approach. Here we integrate these emerging technologies into a unified framework—the generative science of food formulation—in which digital food representations enable AI to predict, discover, generate, organize, simulate, and optimize. We illustrate this approach through sustainability and nutrition, where generative AI transforms environmental and nutritional metrics from post hoc evaluation criteria into explicit design objectives. Finally, we identify the data, models, benchmarks, and automation that will establish computational food design as a rigorous scientific discipline. Together, these advances have the potential to transform food formulation from an empirical discipline into a generative science.
n02e420da49e1: Circadian rhythms regulate the time of day at which various physiological processes take place, including the functions of the kidney. This regulation is made possible by key transcriptional regulators: the core molecular circadian clock, which mediates expression of clock-controlled genes on a 24-h cycle. The present landscape of circadian rhythm research in the kidney spans impacts on the clinical level as well as in basic research, where its role in individual kidney cell types, disease states, and the impacts of environmental stressors is being studied. Recent research has also identified sex differences, cross talk between various tissues, and immune signaling as important considerations for understanding the circadian clocks within the kidney. This review synthesizes the current knowledge of circadian rhythms of the kidney in regard to these issues and stresses the importance of time of day in research as well as in patient health.
nd4adcccfda3e: Probiotics are widely used live microbial supplements intended to promote human health, yet their clinical benefits remain inconsistent and often strain-specific. Most currently available probiotics are derived from Lactobacillus , Bifidobacterium , and Saccharomyces species originally isolated from fermented foods or human microbiota. Preclinical studies suggest that these organisms may influence host physiology through several mechanisms, including antimicrobial activity, toxin inhibition, strengthening of intestinal barrier function, modulation of immune responses, and signaling along the gut–brain axis. However, translation of these mechanisms into consistent clinical benefit has been limited by heterogeneity in probiotic strains, dosing, and study design. Emerging evidence also highlights potential unintended consequences of probiotic use, including rare infections in vulnerable patients, alterations of microbiome recovery after antibiotics, and possible interactions with host metabolism or medications. Recent advances in microbiome research have supported the development of next-generation probiotics and engineered microbial therapeutics, representing a shift toward more targeted and mechanistically informed live microbial therapies.
nbd4a9cbb9721: Flow disturbances in the smallest blood vessels of the brain, the capillaries, have long been considered a potential cause of brain dysfunction. However, owing to the technological challenge of studying blood flow in three-dimensional capillary networks, elucidating the incidence, causes, and consequences of capillary obstructions has been difficult. Advances in optical microscopes for in vivo imaging, primarily high-spatiotemporal-resolution optical coherence tomography and two-photon microscopy, have recently enabled detailed studies of these capillary stalling events in both healthy and diseased mice. In this review, we describe these imaging approaches to quantify capillary stalling, identifying strengths and weaknesses of different methods. We then review recent findings on the incidence, molecular and cellular causes, and physiological and neurological consequences of capillary stalling across multiple mouse models of brain disease, including Alzheimer's disease, stroke, and traumatic brain injury. We conclude by suggesting necessary next steps in instrumentation and analysis for studying capillary stalling, as well as how to address key unanswered questions about underlying mechanisms for capillary stalling in the brain and how this phenomenon may impact disease progression and cognitive function.
na0fff332c64e: Contact angle measurement is a fundamental technique for evaluating surface wettability in materials science, biomedical engineering and coating technologies. However, the high cost of commercial contact angle analysers limits access to surface characterization, particularly in resource-limited laboratories. This study presents a low-cost automated contact angle analyser developed using frugal engineering principles and open-source hardware. The system integrates Arduino-based control, NEMA 17 stepper-motor actuation, automated microdroplet dispensing, smartphone-based optical imaging and a 3D-printed polylactic acid (PLA) framework. A calibrated 330-step dispensing cycle generated reproducible 5 μl water droplets, with fixed optical alignment minimized operator variability. Wettability measurements were performed on polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and aluminium substrates and analysed using ImageJ. Mean contact angles were 108.5° for PTFE, 73.9° for PVC and 85.8° for aluminium, closely matching published literature values. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) demonstrated significant differences between substrates (p < 0.001), with measurement variability of ±2.3° indicated good repeatability. The total fabrication cost was £114.26, representing approximately 99% cost reduction compared with commercial instruments. The proposed platform demonstrates that automated, reproducible surface wettability characterization can be achieved using low-cost, open-source instrumentation, providing an accessible solution for research, education and engineering laboratories while broadening access to advanced materials characterization.
ncefff8df9689: Research on sperm economy has traditionally focused on sperm competition as a major selective pressure shaping sperm production and allocation. In this review, we broaden this perspective by considering how other reproductive and ecological pressures influence the management of a costly and finite sperm supply. We synthesize evidence showing that in externally fertilizing fishes, high mating frequency, low female fecundity, prolonged spawning, rapid sperm dilution and costly male reproductive investment can favour sperm-economy strategies even when sperm competition is weak or absent. Across fish taxa, these constraints have led to convergent behavioural and physiological adaptations, including fractionated ejaculation, temporal matching of sperm release to egg deposition and manipulation of the fertilization microenvironment, which improve fertilization efficiency while minimizing sperm expenditure. We further highlight a recurring association between these strategies and semi-cystic spermatogenesis, consistent with the possibility that optimization of sperm use extends beyond ejaculate allocation to the regulation of sperm production during spermatogenesis. By integrating evidence from behaviour to reproductive physiology, this review reframes sperm economy as a general resource-allocation problem, with sperm competition representing one of several selective pressures. Externally fertilizing fishes emerge as an exceptional model for understanding the diverse evolutionary routes by which males optimize reproductive investment.
n30c157168052: This paper presents an innovative application of two distinct isotope systems to paired otic capsule and outer petrous bone samples from cremated remains. This dual analysis approach, applied to 22 human cremation burials from Roman Colchester (UK), demonstrates evidence for origins outside Britain for several individuals, shedding fresh light on an emerging capital city within a new province of the Roman Empire. Results have implications for understanding the population dynamics of large Roman provincial urban centres following the conquest period in the north-western provinces, when cremation is the dominant burial practice. The method also allows a detailed reconstruction of individual mobility at different ages within an individual's life.
n68c74e424d45: Human sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (hSGLT2) is a membrane-embedded renal transporter and an established therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes. Hyperoside, myricetin, cyanidin-3-O-glucoside and isoliquiritigenin were investigated as a chemically diverse panel of natural scaffolds using a multi-scale computational workflow combining redocking-validated molecular docking, reconstruction of an unresolved transporter segment, molecular dynamics (MD) in an explicit POPC bilayer, molecular mechanics/Poisson–Boltzmann surface area (MM/PBSA) calculations, principal component and free-energy landscape analyses and density functional theory (DFT). The membrane simulations preserved the global hSGLT2 fold while revealing distinct ligand-dependent binding behaviours. Myricetin and cyanidin-3-O-glucoside exhibited limited positional deviations; hyperoside achieved persistent accommodation following an initial adjustment, whereas isoliquiritigenin underwent a marked late rearrangement. Ensemble-based energetic analysis prioritized cyanidin-3-O-glucoside, while hyperoside and myricetin formed an energetically comparable intermediate group and isoliquiritigenin displayed the least favourable profile. Electronic-structure analysis further characterized cyanidin-3-O-glucoside as the most responsive ligand within the DFT subset. Collectively, these findings indicate that glycone-assisted polar anchoring, aromatic complementarity and restricted conformational flexibility promote persistent hSGLT2 recognition. Direct hSGLT2 inhibition and hSGLT1 counter-screening assays remain necessary to establish potency and selectivity.
ned725731fa70: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is a key therapeutic target for various cancers because of its central role in tumor growth and survival signaling. This study employed an integrated computational workflow combining machine learning (ML), molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, umbrella sampling (US), and toxicity prediction to identify potential ALK inhibitors from 307 phytochemicals of the Glycosmis genus. A previously validated CatBoost regression model predicted binding free energies, leading to the selection of 26 compounds with ΔGML < −11 kcal mol−1. Molecular docking identified six top candidates with favorable binding affinities ranging from −5.856 to −9.667 kcal mol⁻¹, which subsequently underwent 200 ns MD simulations. Structural analyses confirmed the stability of all ALK–ligand complexes, while interaction studies revealed extensive hydrophobic contacts and conserved hydrogen bonds involving key ALK residues. US calculations estimated binding free energies from −8.354 to −13.272 kcal mol−1, with compound 54 exhibiting the strongest affinity (ΔGUS = −13.272 kcal mol−1). Several alkaloids, including acrifoline, heptazoline, and atalaphyllidine, also demonstrated promisingbinding properties and reported anticancer activities. Toxicity prediction indicated acceptable safety profiles, highlighting Glycosmis-derived phytochemicals as promising potential ALK inhibitor candidates and supporting the utility of ML-guided virtual screening combined with advanced molecular simulations for natural product-based anticancer drug discovery. Nevertheless, biochemical and cellular experiments are required to confirm their ALK inhibitory activity, selectivity, and therapeutic potential.
na2a1957357f5: Zoonotic disease emergence at the wildlife–domestic animal–human interface results from a complex interplay of ecological, physiological and anthropogenic factors. Here, we have developed a multi-environment, multi-host compartmental model to identify key drivers of spillover risk across urban, rural and natural environments. The framework incorporates heterogeneous host populations, inter-species contacts and host movement, and includes wildlife chronic stress as one factor influencing susceptibility, transmissibility and recovery. Sensitivity analyses show that domestic animal populations at agricultural interfaces strongly amplify spillover risk through their recovery dynamics and per-contact transmission probabilities, while within-wildlife transmission across environments also shapes system dynamics. Chronic stress effects can further increase spillover risk, and the model indicates that reducing wildlife stress alongside improving domestic animal health and management can markedly lower the likelihood of cross-species transmission. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining ecological conditions that reduce chronic physiological stress in wildlife populations and integrating physiological and ecological data into epidemiological modelling. Such models can inform both bottom-up interventions targeting domestic animals and top-down strategies that sustain resilient wildlife communities and, thereby, mitigate zoonotic spillover.
nd67120b48f86: The time it takes for food to transit animal gastrointestinal tracts is essential information to fields from organismal evolution to ecosystem ecology. Nevertheless, current estimation methods do not measure food directly, are impractical for many species and often require unnatural conditions to administer. We overcome these limitations by adopting techniques from organic geochemistry. We trace isotopically tagged greens in lemurs, from ingestion to excretion, through isotopic analysis of higher plant biomarkers recovered in faeces. For frugivorous ruffed lemurs (Varecia rubra), omnivorous ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta) and frugo-folivorous sifakas (Propithecus coquereli), respectively, the biomarkers first appeared at 1.2, 4.3 and 23.4 h after ingestion and peaked at 2.9, 5.7 and 48.4 h after ingestion. These measurements generally match published estimates from pre-existing proxies. However, not all animals cleared the isotopic signal by the end of sample collection, yielding minimum gut retention times of 23.9–29.5 h for ruffed lemurs, 25.5–30.3 h for ring-tailed lemurs and 95.7 h for sifakas. We thus extend gut retention times approximately threefold from pre-existing proxies. Our interdisciplinary approach is applicable across diverse plant eaters, can help refine models of nutrient, seed and pathogen dispersal and be used to probe consequences of lifestyle and medical interventions on organismal nutrition and health.
n9653a9b112e8: The classical maximum entropy principle based on Shannon entropy is widely used to construct least-biased probability distributions from partial information. However, the Shore–Johnson axioms that single out the Shannon functional hinge on strong system independence—an assumption often violated in real-world, strongly correlated systems. When that assumption fails, enforcing the Shannon form imposes an independence the data do not support, and can systematically distort the inferred distribution. We provide a self-contained guide to when and why practitioners should abandon the Shannon form in favour of the one-parameter Uffink–Jizba–Korbel (UJK) family of generalized entropies. After reviewing the Shore–Johnson axioms from an applied perspective, we recall the most commonly used entropy functionals and locate them within the UJK family. The need for generalized entropies is illustrated with two applications, one in economics and the other in ecology. A simple mathematical model worked out in detail further shows the power of generalized maximum-entropy approaches in cases where strong system independence does not hold. We conclude with practical guidelines for choosing an entropy measure and reporting results so that analyses remain transparent and reproducible.
n55c566825d9b: Some soft corals have the potential to increase in prevalence on tropical coral reefs as the severity of anthropogenic climate change increases. While soft corals are therefore an increasingly important component of reef ecosystems, little is known about their ecological role on coral reefs and their influence on community dynamics and diversity. We used Bayesian network inference (BNI) to identify the associations among benthic taxa across sites with varying degrees of soft coral dominance on Fiji's Rainbow Reef, and then employed spatial point process analysis (SPPA) to reveal the ecological processes behind these associations. We found that depth was a dominant driver of community dynamics, and that white Nephtheidae soft corals were negatively associated with scleractinian corals and positively associated with algal proliferation—possibly owing to soft corals reducing grazing pressure. Our results show distinctions in reef benthos and ecological dynamics between scleractinian and soft coral-dominated components of the Rainbow Reef. We found that diversity levels were significantly lower on soft coral-dominated quadrats relative to scleractinian-dominated quadrats, potentially highlighting the reduction in benthic diversity when Nephtheidae soft corals dominate reef walls.
n73bf512be91e: Large language models (LLMs) are generative artificial intelligence (AI) models trained with vast amounts of data and context, and excel at processing, understanding and generating human language, using transformer models to learn statistical relationships between tokens. LLMs are a subset of transformer models, and hence are closely related but not interchangeable. Given the ‘explosion’ of LLM research, the challenge is tracking emerging developments and matching LLMs to applications. This paper reviews LLM developments with the aim of understanding the underlying models’ computational strengths and weaknesses, building on previous work focusing on LLM optimization (Sharkey & Treleaven 2025 Optimising large language models: taxonomy and techniques. SSRN Scholarly Paper no. 5278456. Rochester, NY: SSRN). We find that despite their power, LLMs (transformers) face several key challenges. These include: (i) computational complexity and resource requirements—training and deploying large models is extremely costly and slow, and energy consumption is a concern; (ii) understanding long sequences and dependencies—even with enhancements, models can struggle with very long-range dependencies or context lengths beyond their window (e.g. maintaining coherence in a long document), which reflects the more fundamental absence of continual learning; (iii) interpretability and bias—it remains difficult to interpret why a model produces a given output, and models can inadvertently amplify biases present in training data; and (iv) optimization challenges, including fine-tuning for specific tasks without overfitting or losing generality and ensuring efficient inference (latency, the delay before a response is completed) for real-time applications. In summary, this review focuses on architectural, optimization and interpretability developments in LLMs. It does not aim to provide a systematic benchmark comparison, exhaustive implementation details or empirical performance evaluation, which are covered extensively elsewhere. The authors are committed to updating this review aligned to constant changes in the technology; please reach out with any additions.
n1ddf8a0de09f: The large grove-forming ectomycorrhizal tropical tree Microberlinia bisulcata displays strong mast fruiting on poor soils. Evidence is presented that masting is probably determined primarily by mineral nutrients and secondarily by radiation. To test the nutrient resource limitation hypothesis, phenological recordings were matched with climate variables and modelled using logistic time-series regression. A strong predictor was average daily rainfall in the dry season, low in the current year of masting and high in the year prior. Less strong was the increase in dry season radiation between prior and mast years. Masting events showed no relationship to annual stem increment. Masting intensity was reduced after two caterpillar attacks. Fallen-leaf phosphorus concentration increased in the inter-mast interval, and that for potassium peaked mid-interval. A drier dry season prior to masting may have increased tree carbon, while a wetter one increased nutrient uptake by roots and mycorrhizas. A rooting–fruiting trade-off in carbon is suggested. The long-term stochastic driver appears to be dry season rainfall. Synchrony across masting trees may be enhanced by equilibration of nutrients across the mycorrhizal–root network. A life-history strategy determined by mineral nutrient resource dynamics provides the best explanation and advanced model of the observed pattern of events.
n4a1d2121c02e: Conflict fatalities tend to follow heavy-tailed statistical distributions. A 2005 fusion–fission theory predicts that, when armed groups operate through dynamically forming and fragmenting clusters, the number of fatalities per event should be approximated by a power-law distribution with exponent α near 2.5, with deviations reflecting the relative robustness of larger versus smaller fighter clusters. We use Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) event-level fatality data to estimate α in recent Yemen and Syria conflict periods during 2023–2025. These conflict event datasets are small, incomplete and imperfect and only produce very crude approximations to a power law; nonetheless, the best-fit α values occupy the range 2.5<α<3.5 across most periods, which is broadly consistent with predominantly fragmented or weakly consolidated armed-group organization. Temporary reductions in α are broadly consistent with episodes in which larger coordinated clusters become more consequential. More rigorous testing will require improved datasets to become available in the future.
n591a07844d57: The management of wild bat populations often presents challenges in balancing the needs of biodiversity conservation and public health risks from zoonotic diseases. In Fiji, the most important recognized zoonotic infection is Leptospira, which was recently detected in wild bat populations. Five out of six species of Fijian bats are considered threatened to critically endangered on the IUCN Red List. This study investigates the perceptions of bats by people in Fiji and aims to identify and quantify the reported frequency and types of interactions between bats and people. In this mixed-methods study, 198 Fijian people were interviewed across the three main islands of Fiji: Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and Taveuni. Bats were generally perceived positively (63%, 125/198), mostly because they are perceived to be ‘clean, healthy and tasty’ meat sources (73%, 134/184). The majority of participants consume and come into contact with bats or with their urine, faeces, blood and saliva. Older adults, men and those who recognize that bats can cause harm are more likely to contact bats in Fiji. Quantifying these interactions and identifying other risk factors for bat exposure is an important step in targeting conservation efforts, community engagement and education, as well as determining at-risk groups for possible zoonotic pathogen exposure.
n8dd564363564: Phenological responses to climate warming are well-documented, yet limited data come from low latitudes. Because phenological sensitivity may vary with latitude, studies in low-latitude regions are essential to understand global patterns. To fill this gap, we analysed acoustic recordings collected daily over 15 years on Iriomote Island, in Japan's transitional zone between subtropical and tropical biomes. We applied the BirdNET deep learning model to quantify the breeding phenology of seven frog species. Seasonal calling patterns differed among species, with peaks occurring in various seasons while one species called nearly year-round. Among six species analysed for phenological trends, a winter-breeding tree-frog (Zhangixalus owstoni) showed a statistically significant shift in median calling date (3.8 days later per decade), whereas the other species showed no significant shifts of varying magnitude and direction. Sliding time window analysis indicated late-summer temperature—which increased during the study period—best predicted median calling dates in Z. owstoni, suggesting that climate warming delayed the phenology of a winter breeder even where year-round reproduction is possible. The absence of significant phenological advancement in our dataset contrasts with spring advancement commonly reported in temperate regions. These findings reinforce the importance of examining long-term phenological shifts across more sites in low-latitude regions.
n49315022866a: Violation-of-expectation (VoE) events offer a fascinating lens into the intersection of cognition and emotion. Research suggests that, like humans, many animals are susceptible to VoE events in many physical domains, susceptibility typically assessed through behaviours such as visual and physical exploration of a stimulus. In humans, such susceptibility has been further documented through emotional surprise, such as delight following positive surprise and frustration following negative surprise. However, evidence in animals remains relatively limited. To address this gap, this study examined behavioural, cognitive and emotional responses of capuchin monkeys (Sapajus apella) to bait-and-switch VoE events of food items. Capuchins were chosen for this study not only for their exploratory and information-seeking behaviours, but also for known emotional responses to VoE events (e.g. frustration following inequity aversion). Contrary to prior research, this study found no evidence for violation susceptibility via behavioural, cognitive or emotional responses. Overall, such findings contribute valuable information to the VoE literature in primates regarding methodology and information salience, as well as underscore the current challenges of investigating emotional surprise in animals. Future research may benefit from establishing stronger expectations (e.g. more salient stimuli), to better investigate and quantify surprise to VoE events in animal species such as capuchin monkeys.
n391c1c285e71: Insect cuticles are covered by a complex mixture of cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) that are essential for desiccation resistance and chemical communication, yet the physical structure of CHC layers remains poorly understood. We extracted CHCs from five insect species (desert locusts, house crickets, American cockroaches and two ant species) using solvents of differing polarity and extraction durations, and from insects reared under different temperature regimes. Extractions with n-hexane were enriched in relatively solid CHCs (n-alkanes and terminally branched monomethylalkanes), while extractions with dichloromethane and dichloromethane–methanol yielded proportionally more fluid compounds (internally branched monomethyl and dimethylalkanes, unsaturated hydrocarbons). Solid-phase CHCs were proportionally more abundant in shorter extractions, whereas fluid-phase compounds were proportionally more abundant in prolonged or sequential extractions. These patterns are consistent with a model of cohesive solid domains surrounded by more accessible fluid regions, though this interpretation remains indirect and alternative explanations (e.g. differential solubility and diffusion kinetics) cannot be excluded. CHCs of similar phase behaviour covaried across treatments, indicating that they aggregate within shared domains. Warm acclimatization increased the proportion of solid compounds, whereas fluctuating temperatures enhanced CHCs with intermediate phase behaviour. Our results suggest spatial and chemical heterogeneity in the CHC layer, with patterns of differential extractability consistent with clustering into phase-distinct domains, though direct imaging is required to confirm spatial topology. This potential heterogeneity may facilitate CHC multi-functionality, with the phase behaviour and domain membership of each CHC depending on its biophysical properties relative to the individual's overall CHC profile.
ne744cf225fbf: A dynamical theory of spin relaxation previously formulated in terms of stochastic differential equations is extended beyond the extreme narrowed approximation to incorporate temporal correlation in the driving random magnetic fields. An analysis of spin–spin relaxation in this case is provided, which is non-perturbative in the random field and yields an exact solution to the spin dynamical equations for axial (longitudinal) field fluctuations. We provide a real-time dynamical derivation that leads to a generalized class of spin spectra that are essentially non-Lorentzian for all finite field parameters. A spectral-moment analysis and novel parameter-extraction scheme lead to distinct notions of observable relaxation timescales compared with the standard characteristic exponential. The Lorentzian case is recovered as the extreme narrowed limit.
n65c5456d5af2: Intensive agricultural insecticide use often fails to eradicate pest populations completely, leaving small remnant populations exposed to persistent sublethal residues and potentially elevated inbreeding. How such remnant populations persist remains poorly understood. Here, we examined how inbreeding and sublethal imidacloprid exposure shape survival and post-emergence performance in the Colorado potato beetle (Leptinotarsa decemlineata), a major agricultural pest. We compared four groups differing in breeding status and insecticide exposure history, and quantified emergence rate, locomotor activity, feeding behaviour and reproductive output. We found that despite the insecticide dosage being sublethal, both chemical exposure and inbreeding imposed severe developmental costs, reducing the adult emergence rate with no significant interaction effects. However, among the adults, we observed trait-specific phenotypic plasticity. Male locomotor activity was reduced by both stressors, while female activity remained stable. Notably, herbivory significantly increased under both inbreeding and sublethal insecticide exposure. Furthermore, while inbreeding severely reduced both egg production and hatching success, sublethal exposure to the insecticide surprisingly increased hatching success in surviving pairs. These results demonstrate that sublethal insecticide exposure and inbreeding can create a strong developmental bottleneck. Yet, surviving individuals can exhibit compensatory plasticity that maintains or even enhances their capacity for crop damage.
nfcf55f9c0171: Phytolacca americana L. (Phytolaccaceae), a perennial species native to North America, is rich in oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins. In this study, ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC–QTOF–MS) profiling of the aerial-part extract revealed characteristic fragment ions of phytolaccagenin- and phytolaccagenic acid-type saponins with diverse glycosylation. MS-guided annotation enabled targeted isolation and structural elucidation of two previously undescribed compounds, one oleanane-type triterpenoid saponin (1) and one neolignan (3). Additionally, compound 2, which had been reported only based on mass spectrometric data, was isolated, and its structure was fully elucidated for the first time, together with those of 10 known oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins (4–13). Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive one-dimensional and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic analyses combined with UPLC–QTOF–MS data. Although P. americana extracts have been reported to inhibit influenza A virus infection in previous studies, the bioactive constituents responsible for this antiviral activity have not been identified. The crude extract and isolated saponins were evaluated using complementary in vitro assays. In H1N1-infected A549 cells, compound 11 (3-O-trisaccharide phytolaccagenic acid) reduced viral NS1 RNA levels at 6 and 24 hpi as determined by RT–qPCR. Antiviral activity was further confirmed by plaque reduction and immunoblot analyses, with a plaque-assay IC50 of 57.98 ± 0.26 µM.
nbe8747682f2f: In temperate ecosystems, accessing subtidal environments in the winter is challenging, and therefore, winter ecology and seasonal variation are understudied. For the temperate coral Astrangia poculata, winter is thought to be a period of biological ‘reset’, in which many cellular processes slow or stop, and the microbiome and symbiont community shift dramatically. The period of quiescence, when corals enter a dormant state with limited feeding or metabolic activity, is primarily driven by cold temperatures. However, other ecological drivers of quiescence remain unclear. Here, we documented quiescence in symbiotic and aposymbiotic colonies of A. poculata over a four-month winter period at two depths. First, we confirmed that quiescence is strongly associated with water temperatures under 6°C. Although we quantified a thermocline associated with depth, there was no influence of depth on quiescence. Symbiotic corals were more likely than aposymbiotic corals to enter quiescence, and higher chlorophyll α concentration was associated with lower quiescence, indicating a nutritional link to quiescence in A. poculata. Finally, we compared our results with previous quiescence observations and determined that the dormancy period is shorter in warmer winters, which has implications for the future ecology and behaviour of A. poculata in an era of global change.
ne3f419b56cca: The cell NAD+/NADH ratio can constrain biomass synthesis and influence proliferation in nutrient-limited environments. However, which cell processes regulate the NAD+/NADH ratio is not known. Here, we find that some cancer cells elevate the NAD+/NADH ratio in response to serine deprivation by increasing mitochondrial respiration. Cancer cells that elevate mitochondrial respiration have higher serine production and proliferation in serine-limiting conditions than cells with no mitochondrial respiration response, independent of serine synthesis enzyme expression. Increases in mitochondrial respiration and the NAD+/NADH ratio promote serine synthesis regardless of whether serine is environmentally limiting. Lipid deprivation can increase the NAD+/NADH ratio via mitochondrial respiration in some cells, including cells that do not increase respiration following serine deprivation. Thus, in cancer cells where lipid depletion raises the NAD+/NADH ratio, proliferation in serine-depleted environments improves when lipids are also depleted. Taken together, these data suggest that changes in mitochondrial respiration in response to nutrient deprivation can influence the NAD+/NADH ratio in a cell-specific manner to impact oxidative biomass synthesis and proliferation. Given the complexity of tumor microenvironments, this work provides a metabolic framework for understanding how levels of more than one environmental nutrient affect cancer cell proliferation.
ncf2acaa72e85: Bone marrow (BM) adiposity changes radically through the lifespan, but this phenomenon is poorly characterized and understood in humans. Large datasets of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head have been collected to study the human brain, but also contain unexploited information about other organs. We developed an artificial neural network that localizes calvarial BM in T1-weighted MRI head scans, enabling us to study its composition in several large MRI datasets, and to model sex-dimorphic age trajectories, including the effect of menopause. We revealed high heritability in single-nucleotide polymorphism and twin data, and identified 41 genetic loci significantly associated with the trait, including six sex-specific loci. Integrating mapped genes with existing BM single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed patterns of adipogenic lineage differentiation and lipid loading. Finally, we identified significant genetic correlations with several human traits, including cognitive ability and Parkinson’s disease, which is intriguing in light of the recently discovered channels that link calvarial BM to the meninges.
n1a29ad2a6d47: Aberrant WNT/β-catenin signaling drives tumorigenesis and metastasis in cancer. Although enzymatic inhibitors of tankyrase (TNKS) effectively block AXIN degradation and stabilize the β-catenin destruction complex (DC), they have demonstrated limited efficacy in various colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Here, we demonstrate that, unexpectedly, the induction of AXIN puncta represents a major barrier to achieving therapeutic efficacy. Mechanistically, catalytic inhibition of TNKS prevents TNKS turnover and drives its accumulation in the DC, wherein the scaffolding function of TNKS induces AXIN puncta formation, rigidifies the DC, and impedes β-catenin turnover. Chemically induced degradation of TNKS overcomes this limitation by stabilizing AXIN without puncta formation, providing a deeper suppression of the WNT/β-catenin pathway activity and the proliferation of CRC cells harboring dysfunctional APC mutations. Collectively, these findings provide an explanation for the unsatisfactory outcomes of drugging the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway by TNKS inhibitors and highlight TNKS degradation as a promising approach to treat WNT/β-catenin-driven CRC.
n98b54b00262d: Preleukemia, historically a morphological and cytogenetic diagnosis, is now understood as a continuous clonal process in which somatic mutations, environmental influences, and stem cell pool dynamics interact over decades. Clonal hematopoiesis, the expansion of blood cells carrying somatic mutations, is near-universal in adults over age 70 and confers elevated risk of hematological malignancy, while also acting as a risk factor for cardiovascular and other age-related diseases. Here, we review the genetic and environmental factors that predispose to clonal expansion, organize the mechanisms of clonal expansion into three overlapping and interacting mechanisms (cell-autonomous fitness gain, context-conditional fitness, and nongenetic heritable states), and trace the trajectories that lead from clonal expansion to specific myeloid and lymphoid malignancies. We also discuss methods that have enabled mapping of clonal architecture in human tissue and close on the key questions that we anticipate will define the next decade of research in this field.
n2813c109dab6: Social-class inequities in health arise from power imbalances in our political-economic system. However, through labor-union organizing, workers can build power to improve their life chances and health. In our review, we describe the rich historical, theoretical, and mechanistic evidence linking unions and health and critically evaluate the state of quantitative research on the topic. Most individual-level and ecological studies have estimated small beneficial or null union-health associations. However, as we describe, the studies are limited in number, particularly outside the Global North, and face many technical and conceptual challenges, including feedback loops between unions and societies’ political-economic contexts. We conclude with recommendations for enhancing the rigor and utility of union-health research, including by richly contextualizing studies’ findings and by answering questions raised by workers themselves. As social and economic inequities intensify and workers face heightening attacks on their well-being, unions remain crucial organizations for advancing health justice.
n783a4f8fd667: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This review provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley–Terry–Luce model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from artificial intelligence feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.
n642bd57f6303: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.
n09891904aa78: Insect olfaction is facilitated by a heterotetrameric odorant receptor–odorant receptor co-receptor (OR-Orco) complex. However, extensive sequence divergence and lineage-specific expansion have complicated large-scale comparisons of OR repertoires across insects. Here, we integrated sequence similarity, structural similarity, and molecular docking to analyze ORs from 115 insect species. OR repertoire size was associated with adult diet, larval diet, and habitat, but not with circadian rhythm. We developed a ‘trunk–branch’ network framework to classify ORs according to sequence and structural similarity and used large-scale molecular docking to derive comparative docking profiles. Despite marked differences in sequence- and structural-community composition, almost all sampled orders contained ORs assigned to all six docking-profile communities. Holometabolous insects showed higher OR sequence-community diversity than non-holometabolous insects, and docking-profile composition differed between extant lineages whose order-level origins predate or postdate the end-Permian mass extinction. Most notably, we identified a highly conserved extracellular β-sheet in Orco that restricts ligand access to the binding pocket and may contribute to its reduced capacity to bind natural odorants. The emergence of Orco represents a key evolutionary transition from homomeric receptors to heteromeric OR–Orco complexes, and our results suggest that this transition may have been accompanied by pronounced specialization of the extracellular domain and binding pocket. Together, these analyses provide a class-wide framework for comparing insect OR diversity and generate testable hypotheses for future experimental and evolutionary studies.
n6c6f6731ed94: Tumorigenesis typically follows a multi-hit trajectory, driven by accumulating oncogenic mutations.
